planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring at the shallow, saturated margin of a pond, bog garden, or rain garden basin in full sun to partial shade; bogbean needs constantly wet to shallowly flooded soil and will not tolerate normal garden conditions.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions at the saturated edge of a pond or bog garden, in up to a few inches of standing water, in full sun to partial shade; bogbean is a circumboreal wetland native with distinctive three-part, clover-like leaves held on thick, creeping rhizomes that spread across the surface of shallow water and saturated peat. In late spring, striking spikes of white to pale pink, star-shaped flowers with an unusual fringed, hairy texture on the petal surface rise just above the foliage, a bloom unlike almost any other pond-margin plant. It is a true cold-climate bog and fen specialist, thriving in the cool, consistently saturated, acidic peatlands of the northern United States and Canada, and it does not adapt to drier garden soil no matter how much it is watered. Divide and replant rhizome sections in spring to control spread or establish new plantings, and keep water levels consistent through the growing season.

planting.note: Anchor rooted divisions into muddy or sandy substrate 12 to 36 inches below the water surface of a pond or water garden in full sun to partial shade; wild celery is a true submerged aquatic and will not grow outside standing water.

directions: Anchor rooted plants into soft mud or sandy substrate well below the water surface in a pond or water garden in full sun to partial shade; wild celery is a submerged native aquatic with long, ribbon-like, translucent green leaves that sway gently in current and provide excellent cover and oxygenation for fish and pond life. It spreads by runners across the pond bottom to form dense underwater meadows and is one of the single most important native food plants for migrating waterfowl, particularly canvasback ducks, which rely heavily on its starchy tubers and seeds. Female flowers are carried to the surface on long, coiling stalks for pollination and then draw back underwater to mature, a distinctive reproductive strategy among aquatic plants. It requires clear water with reasonable light penetration to thrive, so avoid excessive nutrient loading or turbidity that would shade out the submerged foliage, and thin congested colonies periodically to keep the planting healthy and open.
